common_name: Kingsville Dwarf Boxwood (Extremely Slow-Growing Miniature Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Kingsville Dwarf is among the slowest-growing boxwood selections known, adding only about a half inch of growth per year, and works well as a true miniature accent, in troughs, or trained as bonsai.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, with protection from harsh winter sun and drying wind in the colder part of its range. Kingsville Dwarf is among the slowest-growing woody plants in cultivation, typically adding only about a half inch of new growth annually and often standing just a foot or so tall after many decades, which has made it a favorite subject for bonsai training as well as a genuine miniature accent for rock gardens, trough plantings, and tiny-scale formal edging where even standard dwarf boxwood cultivars would eventually outgrow the space. Its tiny, densely packed, dark green leaves hold their color well through winter, and the plant needs essentially no pruning to keep its naturally tight, mounded form. Because growth is so slow, start with the largest specimen the budget allows and expect this to be a plant measured in decades rather than seasons.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Boxwood Cultivars

common_name: NewGen Independence Boxwood (Blight-Resistant Modern Hybrid Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; NewGen Independence was bred specifically for resistance to boxwood blight and leafminer, addressing the diseases that have devastated older boxwood plantings across the eastern United States.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. NewGen Independence is one of the first two releases from the NewGen Boxwood breeding program developed by Saunders Genetics, selected specifically to combine strong resistance to boxwood blight (Calonectria pseudonaviculata) with improved tolerance of boxwood leafminer, the two problems that have driven the sharpest decline of traditional English and American boxwood plantings across the eastern United States. It forms a dense, rounded, nearly as-wide-as-tall shrub of deep green foliage that holds its color well through winter, growing at a moderate, predictable pace on sturdy branching that resists snow and ice damage. Provide good air circulation and avoid overhead irrigation to further limit disease pressure, though its bred-in resistance already makes it markedly lower-maintenance than legacy boxwood cultivars in blight-affected regions. Light shearing in late winter or after the spring flush keeps the form especially tidy, though it is not required to hold a good shape.

common_name: NewGen Freedom Boxwood (Fast-Growing Blight-Resistant Hybrid Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; NewGen Freedom grows faster than most traditional boxwood cultivars while retaining bred-in resistance to boxwood blight and leafminer.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. NewGen Freedom is the second release from the NewGen Boxwood breeding program bred by Saunders Genetics for strong resistance to boxwood blight and improved tolerance of boxwood leafminer, and it grows noticeably faster than most traditional boxwood cultivars while still holding a dense, glossy, rounded form that is slightly taller than wide. This quicker growth rate makes it useful where a filled-in hedge or mass planting is wanted sooner than slower-growing boxwood selections allow, without sacrificing the disease resistance that has become essential for new boxwood plantings in blight-prone regions. Expect some winter bronzing in full sun on cold, exposed sites, which fades again with spring growth. Provide good air circulation and avoid wetting the foliage when watering to further limit disease pressure, and shear lightly after the main spring flush if a tighter, more formal outline is wanted.

common_name: Franklin's Gem Boxwood (Cold-Hardy Disease-Resistant Korean Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Franklin's Gem is a Korean boxwood selection valued for exceptional cold hardiness and notably better resistance to boxwood blight and leafminer than English boxwood.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Franklin's Gem tolerates clay, loam, and sandy soils better than many boxwood cultivars. A Korean boxwood selection prized for combining a compact, dense habit with outstanding cold hardiness, Franklin's Gem also shows notably better resistance to boxwood blight and leafminer than English boxwood, making it a dependable substitute where those problems limit other cultivars. Its small, fine-textured, glossy dark green leaves stay green through winter with less bronzing than many hardy boxwood selections, covering a naturally low, dense mound that needs only light shearing to maintain a neat outline. Use it for edging, low hedges, knot gardens, or foundation plantings in climates too cold for less hardy boxwood cultivars.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Boxwood Cultivars
